title: Bhrigu Tests the Three Gods
story:
Which of the three great gods was greatest — Brahma, who made the worlds; Shiva, who unmakes them; or Vishnu, who keeps them safe? The sages who gathered to settle the question could not agree, and argument after argument came to nothing. At last they resolved to settle it not with words but with a test. They chose one of their own, the sage Bhrigu, and sent him out with a single instruction: offer no bow, no hymn, and no word of honor to any of the three, and watch what happened. A god who could not bear a slight, they reasoned, was in the end no greater than the man who offered it.

Bhrigu went first to Brahmaloka, the heaven of Brahma the creator — who happened to be his own father. He walked in and stood before the god and said nothing: no prostration, no praise, not a single syllable of respect. Anger rose in Brahma, hot and gathering, ready to pour out. Then he looked at the man standing silent before him, his own son, and he held it down. He let the insult pass unanswered.

Next Bhrigu climbed to Kailasa, the mountain home of Shiva. Again he offered nothing: no greeting, no honor, no sign that he stood before a god at all. Shiva’s anger did not wait to be mastered. It rose at once, and his trident was already lifting to strike when his wife, the goddess Parvati, threw herself at his feet and spoke soft words to him, and slowly the storm in him went still.

Last of all, Bhrigu came to Vaikuntha, the home of Vishnu. There he found the god lying at ease, the goddess of fortune resting against his chest. Bhrigu walked straight up to him and, without a word, drove his foot into that chest.

Vishnu rose at once from his couch — not to strike back, but to bow. He bent his head to the sage and asked his forgiveness. “Let the touch of the sage’s foot purify me,” he said, “and all who depend on me. Today your foot has made me the one true home of Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune who rests upon this chest.”

Bhrigu stood silent. This was not the answer he had come prepared to receive, and it undid him. He had expected, at best, a god who could master his temper. He had found instead a god who seemed not to have one — who met a blow not with patience but with welcome, as though the foot that struck him had come bearing a gift.

He returned to the assembly of sages and told them what he had seen, and they listened in wonder as the doubt they had carried fell away. In Vishnu, Bhrigu told them, dwelt everything a soul could ask of a god — righteousness, wisdom, and freedom from desire, and the true home of peace and fearlessness. And so the question was answered at last — not by the one who raged, not by the one who mastered his rage, but by the one in whom no rage rose at all.
reflection: The sages set out to measure power and instead measured restraint. Two gods burned at an insult; the third apologized to the foot that struck him — and that, Bhrigu reported back, is where greatness actually lives. The test was meant to find strength, and it found the thing that most looks like weakness: the man who does not hit back.
content_note: Shiva raises his trident in anger, and Bhrigu strikes Vishnu's chest with his foot; no injury is shown.
hero_scene: Bhrigu driving his foot into Vishnu's chest as Vishnu reclines with the goddess Lakshmi, while Vishnu — unhurried, unangered — already begins to rise and bow.
visual_elements: a mood of rising tension turning to calm
